ARTICLE IN PRESS Authentic and Simulated Project-Based Learning to Improve Students’ Employability Skills and Their Translator Competence Abstract Existing project-based learning (PjBL) literature has not covered the differences between authentic and simulated PjBL effectiveness in improving students’ skills. This study investigated whether authentic and simulated PjBL equally improved the translation students’ employability skills and translator competence. This mixed-method study employed documentary analysis and two questionnaires to collect self-report data. Statistical tests were conducted on the result of the first questionnaire to see if authentic projects affected students’ employability skills better than the simulated one did. The analysis of the second questionnaire responses identified students’ most improved translator competence. The findings revealed that both typSes of PjBL equally improved students’ employability skills. However, authentic projects led to more balanced S translator competence improvement. Authentic projects should be preferred as they E improve more balanced translator competence. The authentic PjBL procedure used in the R study also provided a model to bridge university curriculum and industry practices. The P findings emphasize the value of PjBL, particularly authentic PjBL, in translation education so that PjBL is a feasible option for translation curriculum designers and a N preferred learning method when students have got translation basic knowledge and skills. I Using more objective skill improvement measurement, future research is suggested to cover a longer period to see moreE complete improvement and study the long-term impact of the improvement. L C Keywords: project-based Ilearning; emergent competence; translator competence; translation teaching; eTmployability skills R A Introduction Outcome-Based Education (OBE) is applied worldwide. In Indonesia, OBE curriculum is seen as aligned with the Indonesian Education Minister Regulation No 53 of 2023 (Asbari & Nurhayati, 2024). To serve the purpose of education based on the regulation, case-based learning and project-based learning models are advocated. One such implementation was done in an English study program at a vocational college in Indonesia, where authentic and simulated projects were integrated into a translation practicum class. An authentic project is the one assigned by an external translation client, while a simulated project is the one created by the teachers for educational purposes (Chen et al., 2023). This English study program equips students with the core competencies required for in- house translators, particularly focusing on hard skills such as source text analysis, terminology management, CAT tools proficiency, translation quality assurance, and target text revision (hard skills) to prepare them to work after graduation (Politeknik Negeri Malang, 2021). Employers themselves consider hard skills and soft skills to be equally important (Matsouka & Mihail, 2016; Pang et al., 2019). From the research by Matsouka and Mihail (2016), it is known that there are 20 skills expected by industry; together, these are called employability skills. These include (a) learning orientation, (b) extra effort, (c) teamwork, (d) ethics/integrity, (e) ARTICLE IN PRESS communication, (f) professionalism, (g) adaptability, (h) goal setting, (i) emotional intelligence, (j) intrinsic motivation, (k) self-awareness, (l) initiative, (m) creativity and innovation, (n) influence and sales skills, (o) change management, (p) knowledge breadth, (q) academic qualifications, (r) technical skills, (s) global mindset, and (t) leadership skills. In line with the above perspective, Mastela (2023) states that the translation job market nowadays needs translators with holistic competence including linguistic, cultural understanding, technology skills, personal skills, and social skills. Ten years before his proposal, Kiraly (2013) had mentioned that to complete translation tasks well, a translator needs translation competence per se as well as social and personal skills. These complete skills or holistic competences are called professional translator competence (to shorten it, here it is just called translator competence), comprising translation, social, and personal sub-competences. Translation sub- competence includes anything related to linguistic, cultural, text, norms, terminology, world knowledge, strategy, technology and research sub-competences. Social sub-competence consists of etiquette, negotiation, and teamwork. Finally, personal sub-competence consists of ability for autonomy, preparing for lifelong learning, doing quality control, aSnd fulfilling professional responsibility. Li, 2023; Novikova et al., 2019; Xiao & Li, R 2023), showing that it effectively enhanced translation students' real-world skills, including P collaboration, critical thinking, technical competence, and professional identity. However, none has been done to compare the impact of authentic and simulated projects on the improvement of N students’ employability skills and translator sub-competences. This gap led to the need for more I comprehensive, mixed-method research that examined the different effects of the two types of projects on the above skills and sub-comEpetences. Four research questions guided the study: (a) what PjBL procedure was adopted at Lthe practicum course at the research setting, (b) were students’ perceived level of emploCyability skills after the PjBL implementation significantly higher than before, (c) did the auIthentic project drive students’ perceived employability skills higher than the simulated proTject did, and (d) what translator sub-competences were mostly developed with authentic Rand simulated PjBL procedures. Such research would inform curriculum designers iAn structuring the courses and translation teachers in selecting a better translation teaching method. Therefore, using mixed methods, this current research described a PjBL model and investigated the impact of authentic and simulated project-based learning on students’ employability skills and translator sub-competences improvement. Authentic vs simulated project-based learning Projects in project-based learning can be identified as either authentic or simulated projects. An authentic project involves a real project from an external translation client. In such a project, students solve real life problems and are responsible for real life clients outside the classroom (Chen et al., 2023). In contrast, simulated projects are projects created by the teachers for educational purposes. Although they lack real-life engagement, the learning is more controllable. Simulated projects can serve as a stepping-stone for students before working with the professional community in an authentic project or work placement (Chen et al., 2023). Authentic PjBL, which involves external clients withs their real translation assignments, is particularly conducive to developing soft skills (Kiraly, 2005). Students engaged in authentic projects must address challenges in real industry conditions, such as negotiating deadlines, ARTICLE IN PRESS clarifying briefs, handling iterative feedback, and managing expectations from external stakeholders. These experiences require students to demonstrate emotional resilience, adaptability, initiative, and effective interpersonal communications that are central to social and personal sub-competences. Authentic tasks also introduce a degree of unpredictability and complexity that mirrors professional translation work, thereby fostering a deeper sense of accountability and professional maturity. This kind of project has the potential to encourage better students’ engagement and motivation, critical thinking skills, problem-solving ability, and collaboration (Almulla, 2020; Randazzo et al., 2021). This also enhances students’ satisfaction and self-efficacy (Randazzo et al., 2021). This finally helps them prepare for the translation industry work (Paradowska, 2021). In contrast, simulated PjBL does not involve external clients, instead the teacher acts as the client (Kiraly, 2005; Paradowska, 2021). While valuable for foundational skill-building and controlled practice, it typically lacks the external pressure and contextual realism found in authentic projects (Kiraly, 2005). The simulated setting often involves fictitious clients and instructor-designed scenarios, which, although pedagogically usefSul, do not fully replicate the dynamic nature of real-world collaboration. As a result, the opportunities for students to exercise S and strengthen their soft skills—such as conflict resolution, professional etiquette, and decision- E making under uncertainty—are comparatively limited. Therefore, while both types of PjBL R contribute to translation training, authentic PjBL could potentially offer a more robust P environment for cultivating social and personal sub-competences. However, authentic projects are harder to obtain and much more challenging as well as needing much more effort. However, N there is no study investigating whether authentic project worth affording. This current study, I therefore, aimed to see whether authentic projects could improve holistic translator competence better. The results were expected to provEide the translation curriculum designer and translation teachers with insights into the appropLriate PjBL model to boost students’ skills and competences expected by the translation industrCy. I T Project based Learning (PjBL) in translator education R Translation curriculum designers, in response to technological advancements and market A demands, have noted that there has been a gradual shift from traditional teacher-centered to more student-centered, transformational paradigms, which encourage collaborative learning and emphasize the importance of context in developing translation competence (Paradowska, 2021). One method that is in line with this is PjBL, a student-centered learning method which emphasizes learning by doing (D. Li et al., 2015), by producing an end product. The end product may be a published translated document that reflects their understanding and practical competencies (Al-Kamzari & Alias, 2025). PjBL also holds significant potential in fostering the development of emergent competence in translator training (Kiraly, 2006) and to cultivate translation professional skills and competencies (Mitchell-Schuitevoerder, 2013; Neves, 2022). The literature also shows that PjBL has the potential to augment translation training and foster the development of translation skills (Novikova et al., 2019; Xiao & Li, 2023). Thus, PjBL has the potential to improve translation training results. The significance of implementing a project-based method in translator training has been explored by Hutardo Albir (2015) who offered a structured framework for cultivating targeted skills. The study emphasized the importance of a task and project-based methods for translator training. However, the project was only simulated project, which is designed to integrate various ARTICLE IN PRESS elements of learning, including objectives, content, methodology, and assessment. Muam (2017), employing qualitative approach, studied the learner’s perception and opinion towards the advantages of PjBL in a translation course at a vocational education institution. The findings revealed that, according to the students, PjBL in the translation course gave them many advantages, especially in equipping them with conceptual knowledge and its workplace implementation. However, this study did not mention the project procedure and the kind of project completed by the students. Moghaddas & Khoshsaligheh (2019) investigated the effectiveness of Project-based learning (PjBL) in an English-Persian translation class. Adopting mixed method research approach with focus group discussion, participant observation, audio recording, and questionnaire to collect the data, this study revealed that the students’ attitudes toward PjBL were positive; and their translation quality, critical thinking and teamwork skills also improved. The limitation was this study used authentic project only. Then, using questionnaire and reflective jurnal written by the students, Astuti et al (2021) investigated students’ perceptions of the benefits of PjBL in translation class. The finding showed that,S according to the students, PjBL improve their creative thinking, collaboration, English skills. However, the study did not S mention the type of projects and how the classroom procedure was implemented. Using only interviews, the study aimed to explore the students’ N perspectives on growth areas. They found that project-based learning was a key method for developing professional competencies in translation, particularly through international partnerships. Then, Li (2023) investigated PjBL integration into classroom learning, where students participated in a project with a film and TV corporation. The students reported that they improved their translation skills, especially in teamwork and problem- solving. The student selection made her method not applicable in most situations where teachers could not select the students. Xiao and Li (2023) studied the influence of PjBL on improving students’ translation competence in medical English - Chinese translation project. They found that the most improved competence types were specialized knowledge (medical terminology, context mastery), and instrumental competence (effective use of translation tools and research methods). In addition, ARTICLE IN PRESS they also observed significant progress in linguistic competence (handling of complex sentences and technical jargon) and cognitive competence (improved analytical skills for ambiguity resolution). The students also revealed heightened professional identity and confidence in navigating specialized translation tasks. Using mixed-methods case study, they found that the 6th-semester students developed self-directed research and problem-solving skills, improved ability to analyze linguistic and cultural nuances, and enhanced teamwork through group translation projects. However, the source for translation projects was local legends or folktales. This raised questions about the representativeness of the selected texts for various text types potentially faced by students. This limitation could affect the generalizability of the findings for Indonesian - English translation. Emergentist approach in translator education curriculum In the context of translator education, Kiraly and Piotrowska (2014) have introduced the emergent competence theory, a framework that builds upon Dreyfus's (2004) concept of competence acquisition and complexity theory principles. This theory emphasizes the significant role of context in the dynamic, self-starting, and self-sustaining learning process (Guile & Wilde, 2024; Hager & Beckett, 2024). Therefore, translation students should engage in various translation tasks that should be supported with, for example, access to relevant materials, teacher’s and peer’s help, a conducive learning environment, and their own personal and interpersonal dispositions. As students work on these translation tasks, they synthesize their ARTICLE IN PRESS knowledge and skills (Su & Li, 2023). This process helps them gradually progress from the novice translator level to the expert practitioner level. This is the essence of emergent competence theory in translation education. Kiraly and Piotrowska (2014) additionally suggest a model of a translation curriculum that encompasses different phases of learning and teaching. The initial phase is characterized by conscious, less contextualized learning and teacher-centered instruction. As the phases unfold, the learning shifts toward more intuitive, contextualized learning, and the teaching is increasingly more constructive and authentic. The teaching mode evolves from traditional teacher-centered instruction to scaffolded problem-based teaching, project work, internships, and finally the students work in a workplace after graduation. This progression is similar to the sequence of the five stages of adult skill acquisition proposed by Dreyfus (2004). The stages include novice, advanced beginner, competence, proficiency, and expertise. Massey and Kiraly (2021), building on this foundation, recommend an emergent approach to developing translation expertise. Within this approach, translation expertise is developed through compatible stages of learning to facilitate the translation expertise development. KiralyS (2013) takes a metaphor of a vortex to illustrate the developmental process of translator sub-competence. All sub-competences S develop around several vortices (developmental process) as the students do translation tasks and E complete projects. And to complete the task and the projects, they are facilitated with human R resources around them, their personal and interpersonal disposition, and the learning P environment. The interplay of the processes (vortices) co-determines their competence development. The general idea covering the principles that interaction of simple individual parts N eventually develops more complex system is called emergentist perspective or emergentist I approach (Poll, 2011). Kiraly’s (2013) emergentist apprEoach in translator education, however, also raises some problems. Kiraly’s model of vortices Lshows how translators gradually build competence (like "interrelated dynamic vortices"), bCut it does not explain how skills and knowledge, like language, cultural knowledge, technical skIills, and others, work together to facilitate the real translation task completion. Secondly, thTe emergent learning processes might ignore the need for clear lesson plans or proceduresR that could better support translator education. As mentioned by Li (2018) some students sAtill lack basic skills which should be developed before the emergent approach is applied. In addition, the assessment method has never been discussed for the learning model. With unstructured processes, fair assessment for every student might be difficult. Thus, although Kiraly’s ideas are groundbreaking, his model needs more details on how skills are connected to each other and how to balance flexibility with some kind of structures in the classroom. Methodology This case study was conducted at the English for Tourism Industry Study Program at Politeknik Negeri Malang (State Polytechnic of Malang), Indonesia, to examine the effects of the authentic and simulated PjBL procedures on the improvement of students’ employability skills and translator competence. Method This study employed a mixed-method design. The quantitative part was akin to a one-group pre- test-post-test design, with students’ self-assessed employability skills measured using pre- and ARTICLE IN PRESS post-project questionnaires. Participants were selected using a purposive sampling technique, with all students enrolled in the practicum translation course serving as the sample. A Wilcoxon Signed-Rank test was done to determine whether the students’ employability skills improved after following the projects. Additionally, a Mann-Whitney U test was done on IBM SPSS version 26 to see whether the scores gained by the authentic and simulated project groups were significantly different. These non-parametric tests were appropriate due to the relatively small sample size. The qualitative part answered the first and fourth research questions. A documentary analysis of the curriculum document was conducted to answer the first research question, and a content analysis of the students’ responses to the second questionnaire addressed the fourth research question. Sources of data The first source of the data included available curriculum documents (Politeknik Negeri Malang, S 2021), including the course syllabus, learning outcomes, semester teaching plan, assessment S rubrics, and program structure outlines as well as project guides. The second source of data comprised 21 students of the translation practicum class calEled Translation and Hospitality Project Course (2023 academic year) at the English for RTourism Industry Department of Politeknik Negeri Malang, Indonesia, as the respondePnts. Before taking the projects, these students had completed a series of prerequisite tran slation courses, i.e. Introduction to Translation, General text Translation, IT for TraNnslation, Translation for Tourism Industry, Translation for Tourism and Hospitality LegaIl Text, Subtitling for Tourism Industry, and Localization and Transcreation. Two students did not respond to the second questionnaire and E were excluded from the final sample. The sample was taken purposively as this was the only L class taking the Translation Practicum Course. C Ethical considerations were addressed throughout the study. All participants were I informed about the purpose of the study, and written consent was obtained at the time just before T they responded to the questionnaire. Participation was voluntary, and their confidentiality was R assured, and they could withdraw at any time without penalty. To protect the participants’ A privacy, all responses were anonymized. Instruments The effects of the project-based learning here were measured from students’ perception instead of using independent evaluators. Students’ perception was selected because it was difficult to measure improvement in personal sub-competences during the two months’ period with students working in various places. The students’ perception was collected through questionnaires which were distributed on paper sheets in class. The use of questionnaire to draw self-report responses from the respondents followed most of the previous studies in the same topic. This instrument was used as it was difficult to observe students’ improvement on unobservable things such as personal sub-competence. Observation theoretically could be used to see the translation and social sub-competences. However, with five groups working in different places and at different times, observation was not practical in this study. Two questionnaires were used to collect the data. The first one, comprising closed-ended items, was developed based on research findings regarding skills required by companies from fresh graduates (Matsouka & Mihail, 2016). It was to assess the level of employability skills of ARTICLE IN PRESS the students. The 19 items were adapted directly from the list of skills employers sought from fresh graduates (Matsouka & Mihail, 2016), excluding the item on academic qualification. This item was excluded because all participants were at the same level of education (sixth semester). However, the wordings of the items were adjusted for translation-related jobs. This questionnaire was given before the project and given again after the project to compare the result. The complete list of statements on the questionnaire can be found on Supplementary Table - Appendices online. Before being used in this study, the first questionnaire was tried out on 30 students from two classes of a different study program, English for Business and Communication Study Program at the same institution. The validity of the questionnaire was calculated using Pearson Product Moment on IBM SPSS version 26 (IBM Corporation, 2019). The result showed that all items correlate significantly to each other at 0.01 significant level, indicating that the questionnaire was valid. The internal consistency reliability of the questionnaire was calculated using the correlation matrix on the same software application. The Cronbach’s alpha criteria were used to establish the internal consistency reliability, where αS<0.5 was unacceptable, 0.5<α<0.6 poor, 0.6<α<0.7 acceptable, 0.7<α<0.9 good, and α>0.9 excellent (George & Mallery, S 2003; Muijs, 2022). The calculation result showed that the Cronbach’s alpha was 0.964. E The second questionnaire was given after the project. It consisted of two open-ended R questions to collect data on the most developed translator sub-competences. The first question P asked about what skills were improved the most after the project and the second question asked them to write about what new skills or knowledge and what benefit they got during the project. N The questionnaire intentionally avoided referencing translator sub-competences directly to I prevent leading responses and to ensure that students reported only areas of genuine perceived development. The intercoder reliability wEas calculated to see its Krippendorff’s Alpha value (K- Alpha), a measure frequently used forL measuring intercoder reliability for various data types, including nominal data types (MarCzi et al., 2024; O’Connor & Joffe, 2020). The K-Alpha was calculated using the K-Alpha caIlculator developed by Marzi et al. (2024), resulting in K-alpha of 0.915 or 92% agreement. ThiTs level of agreement is acceptable for intercoder reliability. The intercoder reliability measRure can be seen on Supplementary Table -Appendices online. A Data Analysis The documentary analysis of the curriculum document was conducted to identify the authentic and simulated project-based learning procedures implemented. The results of the first questionnaire were analyzed quantitatively. The data on the students’ perceived level of employability skills before and after the PjBL session were compared with Wilcoxon Signed- Rank test on IBM SPSS version 26 (IBM Corporation, 2019) to see if the level after the project session was significantly higher than that before. The difference between the skill level scores after and before was the employability skill gain scores. The scores gained by the authentic and simulated project groups were compared using Mann-Whitney U test on IBM SPSS version 26. Then, content analysis, as the qualitative part, was done to the responses to the second questionnaire. First, the sentences containing the data were extracted and copied into a Word file. The extracted sentences were then coded in line with the competence categories. The code (TC- WK), for example, means Translation Competence - World Knowledge). This code is inserted after a relevant unit of meaning. See Appendix 2 for the complete codes. Finally, two coders identified what skills were mostly developed by each student. ARTICLE IN PRESS Results Project types and the PjBL Procedure The document analysis revealed that there were two types of projects adopted in the course: simulated and authentic. The students were assigned simulated projects if they were unable to secure authentic projects within two weeks of the course’s commencement. They worked in groups of four or five, with one student acting as the project manager, and the others taking on roles as translators and an editor. For the translation projects, two groups (9 students) completed a simulated project to localize an Indian tourism website from English into Indonesian, and three groups (12 students) did authentic projects to translate a restaurant menu, museum website, and museum collection description from Indonesian into English. They were not paid for the project. However, only 8 students of the simulated projects and 11 students of the authentic projects filled in the items of the second questionnaire. Thus, the total number of respondents was 19. From the documentary analysis, the procedure of the PjBL implementation were S identified. The projects required each group to work as a translation team. The role of the S students and the teacher is summarized in Table 1. E Table 1. Roles in the PjBL for translation projects. For the authentic ones, the teacher acted solely as a translation consultant. Student 1, the project manager, organized the first meeting to discuss the project and the deadline. He/she also appointed an editor to record the minutes of the meeting and serve as the group secretary. Subsequent meetings were called as necessary. The flow of work by the group went as follows. Finally, the client used the translation based on the predetermined purpose. For the simulated projects, the steps went almost the same as the authentic project did. The small sample size and the one intact group might affect the generalizability to broader populations of translation students. Discussion The results of the study revealed that both authentic and simulatedS PjBL types were adopted in similar ways, with the client and teacher respectively serving aSs the participant giving the projects to the students. In both projects, students took on various roles, i.e., project managers, E editors, and translators. The teacher also became their consultant for both authentic and R simulated projects. At the beginning of the course, a project guide was agreed to by the class, and P at the beginning of a project, a project plan was agreed by the project group members. The project procedure prescribed in the curriculum dNocument seemed to respond to Massey’s (2019) suggetion that the project pre-requisites, structures, and procedure should be set by the institution I and Siregar’s (2021) concern that a good Pj BL program should have a clear guideline. E The improved translator competence L Both simulated and authentic projeCcts indicated improvement of translation, social, and personal sub-competences. One of the imIprovements in the translation sub-competence reported was the improvement in the students’T vocabulary and knowledge about how to translate a particular text type. They also gained a gRreater understanding of translation methods and skills. These findings were the same as the fiAndings reported by by Moghaddas and Khoshsaligheh (2019) and Insai (2018). The students’ improved knowledge about how to translate is similar to Muam’s (2017) study, which looked into conceptual knowledge. The improvement in their conceptual knowledge is also comparable to the results of Insai’s (2018) study, which found significant improvement of problem-solving capacity. Students’ responses to the second questionnaire indicated that the course helped them develop various communication, time management, teamwork skills, and office bureaucracy skills—such as preparing formal documents, following administrative procedures, and adhering to institutional protocols. Students had to work in groups to tackle shared problems and finally present the result. This collaborative environment helped them develop essential social- interpersonal skills, as they must articulate their ideas, negotiate solutions, and provide response and feedback to peers and clients (Alexandersen et al., 2025; Novalia et al., 2025). These findings were the same as the findings reported by Insai (2018), Moghaddas and Khoshsaligheh (2019), Apandi and Afiah (2019), and Astuti et al. (2021). All these skills were essential in professional translation settings and provided them with increased confidence as reported by some of the students. These results suggest that the students were able to evaluate their own capabilities and take on challenges coming their way in real life. ARTICLE IN PRESS The improvement of all those sub-competences also showed that translator competence could emerge and improve from the project completion process, as affirmed by Kiraly (2012) and Massey and Kiraly (2021). Then, this affirms the concept of emergent translator competence. Authentic and simulated projects The findings revealed a nuanced pattern in the development of translator sub-competences based on project type. Specifically, students engaged in authentic project-based learning (PjBL) procedures demonstrated greater gains in social and personal sub-competence, whereas those involved in simulated PjBL exhibited higher improvement in translation sub-competence. Authentic projects, by their very nature, expose students to real clients, real deadlines, and real communicative stakes—conditions that reflect the social ecology of professional translation practice (Kiraly, 2006; Kiraly & Hofmann, 2019) or commonly called industry realism. Such contexts necessitate interpersonal negotiation, collaboration, and adaptive problem-solving, all of which contribute to the development of social sub-competence, a core dimension of translation competence frameworks such as EMT (2S022) and PACTE Group (2005). These findings are also consistent with Neves (2022), who found that authentic S translation scenarios fostered the emergence of social agency, empathy, and collaborative E responsibility. Moreover, as highlighted by Mitchell-Schuitevoerder (2013), authentic translation R tasks encourage the development of reflective, interpersonal, and action-oriented learning habits, P all critical for navigating the demands of contemporary translation work. Alongside social competence, personal sub-competence was also more significantly N developed in authentic projects. Students reported enhanced confidence, motivation, and I responsibility, likely driven by the real-world consequences of their actions and the accountability embedded in client interacEtions. This aligns with Randazzo et al. (2021) and Almulla (2020), who found that autheLntic PjBL environments promoted greater learner ownership, intrinsic motivation, anCd self-regulated learning. The increased cognitive and emotional investment required iIn authentic projects likely contributes to the internalization of professional identity and persTonal agency, key indicators of personal sub-competence. Conversely, studenRts who participated in simulated projects showed greater improvement in translation sub-comApetence, particularly in areas such as terminology management, genre adaptation, and source-target equivalence. This may be attributed to pedagogical control and scaffolding inherent in simulated tasks, which allow instructors to design targeted learning experiences focused on technical skill acquisition (Hurtado Albir, 2015, 2020). Simulated projects afford a structured learning trajectory, where difficulty levels, text types, and feedback loops are carefully calibrated to instructional objectives. Such environments provide students with opportunities to rehearse translation strategies, apply theoretical models, and receive formative feedback, all of which are essential for consolidating core translation skills (D. Li et al., 2015). Unlike authentic tasks, which often contain unpredictable elements and require learners to divide attention between multiple competencies, simulated projects allow for focused practice on translation micro-skills without the added pressures of client relations or deadline negotiations. These findings support the claim by Chen et al. (2023) that simulated projects act as a transitional stage for developing foundational competencies before learners move on to more complex, real-world challenges. Furthermore, Kiraly and Piotrowska (2014) note that scaffolded classroom environments are particularly effective in early-stage translator education, where the ARTICLE IN PRESS cognitive load of managing linguistic and pragmatic factors may be overwhelming when compounded by social and emotional demands. Industry realism and cognitive challenge Industry realism refers to real-life situations in industrial settings. Authentic projects and simulated projects affect translation, social, and personal sub-competences differently, maybe due to this industry realism, which poses some specific cognitive challenges for the students. Authentic projects, which involve real-world tasks and external clients, provide students with a unique opportunity to engage in negotiation and collaboration that closely mirrors industry practices. For instance, students working on authentic translation projects develop their service provision competence and interpersonal skills as they interact with actual clients and manage real expectations (Paradowska, 2021). This exposure to industry realism enhances their understanding of professional dynamics, as they learn to navigate client relationships and project requirements effectively (Paradowska, 2021). Industry realism plays a crucial role in shaping social competence outcomes in authentic translation projects by pSroviding opportunities to engage in real-world work that increase their interpersonal skills and collaborative abilities. S In contrast, simulated projects, while beneficial for practicing technical skills, often lack E the same level of industry realism. Students in simulated translation projects may engage in R collaborative tasks, but the absence of real clients can limit the depth of negotiation, and the P stakes involved. Although these projects allow for the development of project management skills and teamwork, they may not fully replicate the complexities and pressures of real-world N translation work, which can affect the development of social competence. I The cognitive challenges also differ in the two types of projects. Authentic projects often present students with unpredictable scenEarios that require critical thinking and problem-solving in real-time, fostering a deeper cognitLive engagement (Novalia et al., 2025). This environment encourages students to adapt and iCnnovate, enhancing their personal competence as they learn to manage stress and uncertainty (PIaradowska, 2021). On the other hand, simulated projects may provide structured tasks that,T while useful for skill development, do not always push students to the same cognitive limits,R potentially resulting in a less robust development of personal competence. MoreoveAr, the cognitive challenges presented in authentic projects, such as dealing with unexpected client feedback or project changes, further contribute to the development of personal and social sub-competences. Students learn to adapt their communication styles and negotiate effectively, which are essential skills in the translation industry (Novalia et al., 2025). In summary, the industry realism in authentic projects significantly enriches the social competence outcomes for students, preparing them more effectively for the collaborative nature of professional translation work compared to simulated projects. This study, while offering valuable insights, was subject to limitations. First, the sample size was relatively small. This affected the applicability to more varied students’ characteristics. Second, the duration of exposure to each project type was limited to two months, which might not capture complete and long-term competence development. This relatively short timeframe could not be sufficient to fully capture the progression or sustainability of, for example, the translator competence that typically evolve over a longer period. Third, the sub-competence gain was assessed through self-reported reflections, which could have introduced subjectivity or self- report bias. In fact, although such qualitative data could offer free and open perspectives, they might be influenced by the tendency to present oneself in a favorable situation, which might not align with objective reality. Fourth, the study did not control the work focus and criteria given by ARTICLE IN PRESS the client and the teacher. This might have caused the differences in the students’ sub- competence development. Finally, the self-reported data might have caused this study to be unable to confirm the development of critical thinking skills. None of the participants referred to these skills in their responses to open-ended questionnaires. Although this was one limitation of the study, this absence was consistent with findings from previous research by Matsouka and Mihail (2016), Moghaddas and Khoshsaligheh (2019), and Apandi and Afiah (2019), which similarly reported limited evidence of creativity and critical thinking skills development. Conclusions and Implication Based on the findings, several conclusions can be drawn regarding authentic and simulated PjBL. The implication is stated after each conclusion. First, the PjBL method implemented in the English for Tourism Industry Study Program of Politeknik Negeri Malang, Indonesia, accommodated authentic and simulated projects. The students worked in groups and played different roles like those in translation offices, mirroring the dynamics of real-world S environments. A project guide was set given before the PjBL started and the students created a S project plan after the project was obtained. It implied that the PjBL procedure could serve as a model to follow in the teaching of translation practicum couErses at universities, especially at vocational colleges preparing ready-to-work graduates. R Second, this study demonstrated that both autPhentic and simulated Project-Based Learning (PjBL) procedures effectively improved s tudents' employability skills, with no significant difference in the employability skill Ngain. This finding emphasizes the value of PjBL in translation education, particularly in preparIing students for real-world working environments. The implication is that translation teachers have options to help students develop their readiness E for translation work; they can choose either authentic or simulated projects to bring into their L classrooms. C Third, the findings also demonstrated that authentic projects produced more balanced I translator competence development. This suggests that authentic projects have their potential as a T preferred method for nurturing holistic translator competence. Therefore, translation teachers R should bring authentic projects into the classrooms. As authentic projects may not always be A feasible due to constraints such as limited access to industry clients, time restrictions, or institutional regulations, the teachers can enhance the simulated projects to resemble the authentic ones. For example, educators can design tasks based on real client briefs for similar texts, set realistic deadlines and revision processes, and assign team roles that reflect actual workplace dynamics. This is the implication of the fourth limitation mentioned previously. In addition, simulated interactions with ‘mock clients’, such as email exchanges or scheduled meetings, can also be used to promote interpersonal and negotiation skills. Reflective elements, such as peer reviews and self-evaluations, can be introduced to help build the kind of professional accountability and critical thinking expected in industry settings. By embedding these features, simulated projects can better support the development of both technical skills and the soft skills essential for professional translators. Another implication for the curriculum designers is that they need to incorporate PjBL into their course structures and restructure the translation courses in such a way that they culminate in a course applying authentic project-based learning. Simulated projects can be used in early stages of translator education to build foundational skills and confidence, while authentic projects can be introduced progressively to foster social maturity and real-world adaptability. Next, as manager roles have specific improvement in etiquette skills and leadership skills, ARTICLE IN PRESS teachers should rotate the role every time a new project commences. To give more opportunities to more students, project length could be shortened to 4 weeks. In relation to the methods of this current research, some weakness produces suggestions for future research. The instruments in this study were questionnaires only which were prone to bias. Therefore, future studies utilizing observation or other assessment methods need to be conducted to see the effect of PjBL on the improvement of students’ translator competence more objectively. Next, this study was done in two months’ time-period only so that the sub- competences development might not be full yet. Therefore, it is recommended that future research observes the phenomenon in longer period of time. Additionally, future studies could investigate the long-term effect of authentic and simulated PjBL on the students’ career growth and performance in the translation industry. JSON: Name: authentic_simulated_pjbl_translator_competence Title: Mixed-method comparative evaluation of authentic versus simulated project-based learning for improving translation students' employability skills and translator competence Short Hypothesis: Exposure to authentic project-based learning (PjBL) produces significantly larger gains in students' social and personal translator sub-competences and yields a more balanced overall translator competence profile than exposure to simulated PjBL, while simulated PjBL produces equal or greater gains in translation (technical) sub-competence. Related Work: Prior work demonstrates that project-based learning (PjBL) in translation education improves translation quality, teamwork, terminology management, and professional identity. Existing approaches fall into two clusters: (1) simulated PjBL implemented as instructor-designed, scaffolded tasks that target technical translation micro-skills and controlled practice; and (2) authentic PjBL that embeds real clients, deadlines, and stakeholder interactions to approximate industry conditions and promote interpersonal, negotiation, and self-regulatory skills. Limitations across the literature include reliance on single text types or single-case contexts, small and non-random samples, short exposure windows, predominant use of self-report measures, sparse use of blinded objective quality assessments (e.g., post-editing/Human-targeted metrics), and lack of direct comparisons between authentic and simulated PjBL within the same instructional design. No consensus exists on whether industry realism (authenticity) or pedagogical scaffolding (simulation) is superior for producing balanced translator competence, and prior studies seldom combine objective client- or rater-based outcomes with validated employability or behavioral metrics. Abstract: This research compares authentic and simulated project-based learning (PjBL) for developing employability skills and translator competence in undergraduate translation students. We propose a mixed-method experimental pipeline that (a) randomly assigns students to authentic-PjBL (real external clients), simulated-PjBL (instructor-designed client scenarios), or a teacher-centered control; (b) measures pre/post changes using objective translation quality metrics (post-edit distance, terminology accuracy), blinded rater scores, validated employability and sub-competence scales, and behavioral logs (negotiation exchanges, revision counts); and (c) collects qualitative data from client feedback and student reflections. The main contribution is a reproducible experimental protocol that isolates the effect of industry realism on social, personal, and translation sub-competences and evaluates convergence between self-report and objective measures. Expected outcomes are (1) authentic PjBL will produce larger gains in social and personal sub-competences and a more balanced competence profile, (2) simulated PjBL will yield greater or equivalent improvements in translation-specific technical measures, and (3) objective metrics will reveal divergences from self-reported gains. The pipeline informs curriculum design and assessment choices for translator education. Experiments: Design: three-arm cluster-randomized trial with mixed methods. Participants: N=120 undergraduate translation students (power analysis target: d=0.7, alpha=0.05, power=0.8) allocated to authentic-PjBL (n=40), simulated-PjBL (n=40), control teacher-centered instruction (n=40). Grouping: teams of 4–5 (8–10 teams per condition); role rotation (project manager, translators, editor) each project. Duration: one academic semester (12 weeks) with two sequential projects (each 5 weeks + 1 week assessment). Materials (datasets/texts): four text genres per project set (tourism website, restaurant menu, museum/object description, short legal notice) balanced for length (~300–800 source words) and difficulty; each team translates two texts (one per project). Baselines: teacher-centered lecture/practice; simulated-PjBL uses instructor-created client briefs and internal feedback loops; authentic-PjBL uses external clients supplying real briefs and feedback. Evaluation metrics (pre and post, plus 6-month follow-up): (1) translation quality: blinded rater adequacy/fluency Likert 1–7 (two independent raters, inter-rater ICC reported), HTER (human-targeted edit distance) measured by post-editing performed by professional post-editor, terminology accuracy (% agreed key terms), and turnaround time (minutes); (2) employability and sub-competence scales: validated multi-item instruments adapted from employer-skill taxonomies mapped to translation social/personal/translation sub-competences (Cronbach's alpha reported); (3) behavioral metrics: number of client interactions, negotiation messages, number of revision cycles, on-time delivery rate; (4) client satisfaction: standardized client rating (1–7). Qualitative data: semi-structured client interviews, student reflective journals, and focus groups. Analysis: mixed ANOVA (condition x time) for continuous measures, non-parametric tests if assumptions violated, pairwise contrasts with Bonferroni correction, effect sizes (Cohen's d), multilevel modeling to account for team clustering, mediation analysis to test whether behavioral metrics mediate competence gains. Ablations/comparisons: (A) simulated-PjBL with and without instructor role-playing as client (to isolate client realism), (B) authentic-PjBL with variable client engagement intensity (low vs high feedback frequency), (C) objective metrics vs self-report concordance analysis. Pre-registration: specify primary outcomes (social sub-competence gain, translation HTER) and analysis plan. Risk Factors and Limitations: Technical and measurement risks: self-report bias and social desirability in employability scales; assessor bias despite blinding; inter-client variability creating noise in authentic condition; limited sensitivity of some objective metrics (e.g., HTER may not capture stylistic adequacy). Data risks: uneven team formation or attrition reducing power; contamination between conditions (students sharing materials). Scalability and resource constraints: recruiting sufficient external clients and professional post-editors, and time cost of blinded rating and post-editing. Generalization limits: findings may not generalize beyond the sampled institution, languages, or chosen text genres; vocational program context may differ from research university settings. Temporal limits: semester-long exposure may be insufficient to capture long-term competence consolidation or career outcomes. Ethical/legal risks: client data confidentiality and copyright for authentic materials. Statistical risks: clustering effects and non-independence of observations may reduce effective sample size; multiple comparisons inflate false positive risk if not controlled.
